slide.title: From 40 Ideas to 8
slide.body: A funnel: many small grey idea cards at the top, eight teal cards at the bottom. Small tag: AI for Content Creators · Lesson 4.

scenes.voiceover: Getting forty content ideas from AI takes less than a minute. Choosing the eight that are worth making takes real thinking. This lesson is about both halves. And the second half is the one that matters.

slide.title: Vague or structured?
slide.body: Left, grey: 'Give me content ideas for my gym' → generic ideas. Right, teal: prompt with pillars, formats and customer questions → specific ideas.

scenes.voiceover: You now have a voice guide and a persona. Let's use them to find ideas. AI assistants are very good at producing many ideas quickly. But the quality depends on the structure you give them. A vague prompt, like give me content ideas for my gym, returns ideas that any gym could post.

slide.title: Three frameworks
slide.body: Content pillars: 3–5 main themes · Formats: short video, carousel, poll, behind the scenes, newsletter · Customer questions (next)

scenes.voiceover: A structured prompt gives the AI a framework. Here are three useful ones. Content pillars are the three to five main themes your brand talks about. Formats are the types of content you can make, such as a short video, a carousel or a poll.

slide.title: Add what you already know
slide.body: Real customer questions → post ideas · + Voice guide (Lesson 2) · + Persona (Lesson 3)

scenes.voiceover: And customer questions are the real questions people ask you. Ask the AI to turn each one into a post idea. Then add your voice guide and persona, so the ideas fit your brand and your audience.

slide.title: The three-point filter
slide.body: Idea card passes three gates, each scored 1–3: Fits the brand · Useful to the audience · Possible to produce → Total out of 9. Note: tie? pick the most different idea.

scenes.voiceover: Then comes the filter. Score every idea from one to three on three criteria. Does it fit the brand? Is it useful to the audience? And is it possible to produce, with your time, budget, skills and permissions? Add the scores and keep the highest. When scores are equal, choose the idea that is most different from the rest, so your list has variety.

Think of AI ideas as a large catch from a fishing net. The net brings up many fish at once, but also weeds, stones and fish that are too small. Filtering is the sorting table, where you keep only what you can use.

scenes.stock_query: group fitness class adults studio India
scenes.voiceover: Here is an example. Priya is the marketer for a sample fitness studio in Pune, India. The studio offers group classes for working adults. Her three pillars are short workouts, member stories, and rest and recovery.

slide.title: Priya's structured prompt
slide.body: Using the voice guide below, suggest 40 content ideas for a fitness studio for busy working adults in Pune. Group them under our 3 pillars. For each idea, suggest a format: short video, carousel, poll or story. Also include 10 ideas based on these real member questions: …

scenes.voiceover: She writes a structured prompt with her voice guide. She asks for forty ideas for busy working adults, grouped under her three pillars, each with a format. She also adds three real member questions. Can I join if I have never exercised? What should I eat before an evening class? And how do I avoid knee pain?

slide.title: Scoring the ideas
slide.body: Table with Brand / Audience / Possible / Total: 10-minute desk stretch video 3·3·3 = 9 (green) · Member story: first class at 45 3·3·2 = 8 (green) · 'Celebrity workout secrets' 1·1·1 = 3 (red)

scenes.voiceover: She gets forty ideas in a table and scores them. A ten-minute desk stretch video gets full marks, nine out of nine. A member story about a first class at forty-five gets eight. But celebrity workout secrets gets only three. It is off-brand, and it uses real people she has no permission to feature.

slide.title: Low on 'possible'
slide.body: Meal plan for weight loss 2·3·1 = 6 (amber): no nutrition expert. Knee pain → reframed: 'When to see a doctor about knee pain', general tips from a trainer, clear note to get medical advice.

scenes.voiceover: A meal plan for weight loss scores six. The audience wants it, but it is not possible to produce well. The studio has no nutrition expert, and diet advice without one could be unsafe. The knee pain question becomes a different idea: when to see a doctor about knee pain, with a trainer giving general tips.

slide.title: The shortlist: 8 ideas
slide.body: Eight teal cards arranged in three columns by pillar (Short workouts · Member stories · Rest and recovery), each with a small format icon: video, carousel, poll, story.

scenes.voiceover: Priya ends with a shortlist of eight ideas, across all three pillars and four formats. The list is short and varied, and every choice has a clear reason that she can explain to the studio owner.

The most common mistake is to skip the filter and post the first ideas in order. The first ideas are often the most general. And judging only by whether you like an idea is not enough. Clear scores make your choices easier to explain to a manager or client.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Structure prompts: pillars, formats, customer questions. 2. Filter: brand, audience, possible. 3. Short, varied, scored list > long unfiltered list.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, structured prompts using content pillars, formats and real customer questions give more useful ideas than vague prompts. Second, filter every idea on three criteria: fits the brand, useful to the audience, and possible to produce. Third, a short, varied, scored list is worth more than a long list of unfiltered ideas.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, generate thirty ideas for your brand with Claude or ChatGPT. Score each one on the three criteria, and keep your top eight, across at least two pillars and two formats. It takes about twenty-five minutes. In the next lesson, Rules of the Road: Copyright, Disclosure and Accuracy, we look at what to check before you publish. See you there.
